extraction.name: Vibravox: A Dataset of French Speech Captured with Body-conduction Audio Sensors
extraction.description: A GDPR-compliant dataset of French speech and physiological sounds recorded from 188 participants using five body-conduction audio sensors plus an airborne reference microphone, with annotations for recording conditions and linguistic transcriptions. The paper also presents baseline experiments for speech enhancement, speech-to-phonemes recognition, and speaker verification.
extraction.creator: Julien Hauret, Malo Olivier, Thomas Joubaud, Christophe Langrenne, Sarah Poirée, Véronique Zimpfer, Éric Bavu
extraction.citeAs: Hauret, J., Olivier, M., Joubaud, T., Langrenne, C., Poirée, S., Zimpfer, V., & Bavu, É. Vibravox: A Dataset of French Speech Captured with Body-conduction Audio Sensors.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: A recording protocol was designed and implemented to collect simultaneous audio from six sensors per participant in controlled conditions. Participants completed four consecutive recording steps: speech-clean, speechless-noisy, speechless-clean, and speech-noisy. The process used a Zoom F8n recorder, a 3D sound spatializer with 56 loudspeakers for noisy conditions, and dedicated hardware/software for acquisition. A total of 200 participants contributed, and 188 were retained after post-processing.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Physical data collection, Experiments, Manual Human Curator
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Some audio clips had shortcomings such as mispronounced sentences, sensors shifting from their initial positions, occasional sensor malfunctions, or a microphone being inadvertently left unequipped. Some filters did not trigger in cases such as an ear canal too small for proper acoustic sealing.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Simultaneous audio recordings from five body-conduction sensors (in-ear soft foam microphone, in-ear rigid earpiece microphone, throat microphone/laryngophone, forehead accelerometer, temple vibration pickup) and one airborne headset microphone reference; textual reading material sourced from the French Wikipedia subset of Common Voice; ambient noise excerpts sourced mainly from AudioSet plus in-house ambisonic recordings of concerts and street events.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Ambient noise samples were spatialized using the ambitools library and rendered by a spherical array of 56 loudspeakers. Text was filtered to remove proper names, numbers, Greek letters, mathematical symbols, and syntactic errors; text was lowercased and punctuation removed except apostrophes. Phonetic transcriptions were generated with the CoML lab phonemizer and manually corrected for unrecognized words. Post-processing used automatic filters based on phoneme error rate, signal-to-noise ratio, and sensitivity drift; VAD timestamps were extended by 0.6 seconds on both sides and trimmed by 15 ms when needed.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Audio was high-pass filtered at 20 Hz on each acquisition channel. Speech-clean utterances were filtered to retain only correct pronunciation and sufficiently high SNR. The dataset was split by speaker into train/validation/test with no speaker overlap. VAD segments were expanded by 0.6 seconds on both sides, and audio was trimmed by 15 ms when boundaries exceeded original limits.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotations include recording-condition labels and linguistic transcriptions. Text readings were transcribed into phonetic labels using IPA with 33 French phonemes. Manual phonetic transcription was performed for words not handled correctly by the phonemizer. During post-processing, phoneme error rate was computed by comparing labeled phonetic transcriptions with Whisper-derived phonetic transcriptions.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Post-processing used automatic filtering based on PER < 10%, SNR > 1.5 dB, and a drift check comparing speech and silence levels. The paper notes that the filtering excluded 6% of participants and 6.8% of pronounced sentences and was intended to ensure rigorous analysis and fair comparison rather than maximize performance.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Whisper-timestamped, Whisper, dynamic time warping, CoML lab text phonemizer, Voice Activity Detection
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Gender, age, language (French), and participant morphology-related considerations for sensor fitting were discussed; the dataset also includes physiological sounds such as breathing and heart-rate-related signals.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is intended to advance robust communication in noisy environments and support applications such as speech enhancement, speech recognition, speaker verification, voice commands, and monitoring vital signs. The paper also mentions potential military and industrial applications.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The paper notes deliberate efforts to recruit a diverse and gender-balanced group of participants. It also discusses limitations of existing datasets such as restricted languages, limited sensor diversity, and noise/artifact issues, but does not explicitly characterize bias in the released dataset beyond these considerations.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset is limited to French speech and to the specific sensor configurations used. Some sensors have narrow bandwidth or are sensitive to fit issues, and some recordings contain noise, artifacts, or insertion defects. The paper notes that the dataset is not the largest available and that some noisy-condition subsets lack a clean reference, limiting their use for training in certain tasks.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, validation, and testing for speech enhancement, speech-to-phonemes recognition, and speaker verification. The speech-clean subset is the main training resource; speech-noisy is primarily for testing; speechless-clean and speechless-noisy support denoising, augmentation, and physiological/noise analysis.
